notes.meaning: The heading tells us when David wrote this. King Saul sent soldiers to watch David's house overnight so they could kill him in the morning (1 Samuel 19:11). Trapped, David turns to God and asks to be rescued and lifted up, like being set in a high tower out of reach. He sets the words "my God" against "my enemies." Matthew Henry says Christians can pray this daily against temptation and the wrong desires of their own hearts.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars doubt that the heading fits the psalm and place it later. Adam Clarke thought it came from Nehemiah's day, when enemies tried to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Others have suggested a later king of Judah or the time of the Maccabees, Jewish leaders who fought foreign rulers about 150 years before Christ.

notes.meaning: David calls his attackers men who do evil and men who shed blood. Matthew Henry says that makes them enemies of God and of all people, not just of David. Saul had tried to kill David before, so David knew what to expect. His cries pile up: "deliver me," "protect me," "save me." Spurgeon compares them to an alarm bell ringing loudly.

His enemies hide and wait like a wild animal ready to pounce. Powerful men have joined together against him. David says he has done nothing to deserve this. He isn't claiming he never sinned against God. He means he never wronged Saul. Matthew Henry notes that being innocent won't keep good people from trouble, but it is a great comfort in the middle of it.

Saul's men rush about and line up as if for battle, though David has given them no cause. So David asks God to "arise" and come to meet him with help. God never sleeps, but in hard times he can seem to. Plumer notes how eager wicked people are to do wrong, and says this should shame believers who are slow to do good.

David uses names for God that fit his need. "God of Hosts" means God of the armies of heaven, so God is able to help. "God of Israel" reminds God of his promises to his people, so he is willing to help. "The nations" here includes Israelites who acted like pagans. Asking God to "show no mercy" is a cry for justice against people who will not stop doing evil. Matthew Henry says this kind of prayer looks ahead to God's judgment, and is not an example for us to copy. "Selah" probably marks a pause in the music.

David compares Saul's men to the wild, half-starved dogs that roamed Eastern cities in packs at night. Each evening the watchers came back, growling and circling the town so he could not escape. Matthew Henry adds that they spread an outcry against David, calling him a traitor.

Cruel words gush out of their mouths like water from a spring. Their slanders cut like swords. "Who can hear us?" shows they think no one, not even God, is listening. Matthew Henry notes that people who think God doesn't care what they say will stop caring what they say themselves.

They thought no one heard, but God heard, and he laughs at their plans, as in Psalm 2:4. Spurgeon says they laughed at David, but God had the last laugh, sending them away empty-handed. Even the strongest and cleverest enemies of God's people are no match for him.

Saul's men watched David's house to kill him, but David keeps watch for God. He calls God his strength and his fortress, a high, safe tower. Older translations read "because of his strength." On that reading, Saul's great power is the very thing that drives David to wait on God.

"Loving devotion" means God's faithful, never-failing love. David is sure God will come to meet him, even helping before the need arrives. Matthew Henry finds comfort that God is "my" God of mercy, close and personal. Spurgeon says "stare down my foes" means David will look at his enemies calmly and without fear.

David asks God not to wipe out his enemies all at once, because quick punishments are soon forgotten. Instead he asks God to scatter them, like Cain, who was made a wanderer. That way they would be a lasting reminder of God's justice. Calling God "our shield," David speaks for all God's people. Spurgeon calls this a soldier's prayer from a man suffering great injustice.

The enemies' worst sins are sins of the tongue: pride, cursing and lies. David asks that they be caught by their own words, like hunters trapped in their own net. Matthew Henry notes that sins of speech do more harm than we usually think, and that Saul was given to cursing.

This doesn't cancel verse 11. After the enemies have served as a warning, David asks God to bring them to an end at last. Some older writers think he means an end to their power and pride, not their lives. The goal is that the whole world will know God rules over his people and over all the earth.

David repeats the picture of the night dogs. They prowl and hunt for food, and growl when they go hungry. The food they want is David himself, and they can't get it. Some translations say they "stay all night," still hoping to catch him. Matthew Henry also reads it as their punishment: the hunters become hungry and never satisfied. He adds that discontent, not being poor, is what makes a person truly unhappy.

"But I" marks the contrast. The dogs howl in the night, and David sings in the morning. He praises both God's strength and his love. Matthew Henry explains that strength without mercy would be frightening, and mercy without strength couldn't help. The night stands for trouble and the morning for relief. Matthew Henry says that when the night of trouble is over, God's people will sing.

The psalm ends where verse 9 began, but now David sings instead of only waiting. God holds back the strength of the wicked and gives strength to his own people. David takes no credit himself. All his strength, safety and mercy come from God, and so all the praise goes to God.
